Mining of Massive Datasets by
Jure Leskovec, Anand Rajaraman, Jeff Ullman

To extract knowledge, data needs to be
• Stored (systems)
• Managed (databases)

• Data mining = extraction of information from
very large datasets

Data Mining ≈ Big Data ≈
Predictive Analytics ≈ Machine Learning

Descriptive methods
• Describe data in a way that humans can interpret
e.g. Clustering

Predictive methods
• Use some variables to predict unknown future values of
other variables
e.g. Recommender systems
Good news: Demand for data mining

If you look hard enough for a pattern, you are bound to
find it.

We want to find (unrelated) people who at least twice
have stayed at the same hotel on the same day.

•
109 people being tracked
•
1,000 days
•
Each person stays in a hotel 1% of time (1 day out of
100)
•
Hotels hold 100 people each
How many “suspicious” pairs of people will we find?

• Probability of two people visiting a hotel on the same
day is 0.012 = 10−4.
• Probability of two people visiting the same hotel on
the same day is 10−4 ∗10−5 = 10−9.
• Chance that they visit the same hotel together on two
separate days is (10−9)2 = 10−18.
• Number of pairs of people is
109

• Number of pairs of days is 1000
2
≈5 × 105

• Expected number of “suspicious” pairs of people:
5 × 1017 × 5 × 105 × 10−18 = 250,000.

… too many combinations to check – need more
evidence

Takeaway:
• It is reasonable to assume that the running time of a
frequent-itemset algorithm is proportional to the number
of passes through the data (of baskets) times the size of
the data


It is called a pass through the data since the baskets are read in
sequence

Since we cannot control the size of data, we measure the
speed of an algorithm by the number of passes through the
data taken by the algorithm

For many frequent-itemset algorithms, main-memory is the
limiting factor.

•
As we read baskets, we need to count something,
e.g. occurrences of pairs of items
•
The number of different things we can count is
limited by main memory

The hardest problem often turns out to be finding the
frequent pairs of items {i1, i2}
• Freq. pairs are common, freq. triples are rare
o Probability of being frequent drops exponentially

with size; number of sets grows more slowly with size.
• Let’s first concentrate on pairs, then extend to larger
sets

Definition: Formally, a hash function ℎtakes a hash-key
value as an argument and produces a bucket number.
• Let the bucket number be an integer in the range 0 to 𝐵𝐵−1
• Intuitively, hash functions should “randomize” the hash-keys
roughly uniformly into each of the 𝐵𝐵buckets

Simplest Example:
• Let the hash-keys be positive integers, then we can use the
remainder hash function

𝒉𝒉𝒙𝒙= 𝒙𝒙mod 𝑩𝑩


• For more details and examples, see Chapter 1.3.2 of
textbook.

Hashing phone numbers
Sum up the digits modulo 𝐵𝐵
• E.g. 𝐵𝐵= 11, phone number = 836192715218
• Output = 8+3+6+1+9+2+7+1+5+2+1+8 (mod 11) = 9

If the sum tends to be smaller than 𝐵𝐵, we could partition the
phone number into blocks of several digits and concatenate
them before summing modulo 𝐵𝐵
• E.g. 𝐵𝐵= 97, phone number = 836192715218
• Output = 836+192+715+218 (mod 97) = 21

Hashing Strings
We can convert each character to an integer using its ASCII
code, and then use the techniques above

Repeatedly read small chunks of the file into main memory
and run A-priori to find all frequent itemsets
•
Note: we are not sampling, but processing the entire file
in memory-sized chunks

An itemset becomes a candidate if it is found to be
frequent in any one or more chunks.
• Like in the random sampling method, we must adjust the
support threshold proportionally.



support threshold should be reduced to 𝒑𝒑𝒑𝒑

Pigeonhole principle: If an itemset appears at least 𝒔𝒔
times in whole, then it must appear at least 𝒑𝒑𝒑𝒑times
in some chunk of data. No false negatives!

On a second pass, count all the candidate itemsets and
determine which are frequent in the entire dataset, to
remove false positives.

• Pros:  Avoids false positives and negatives
• Cons: Have to run through entire file in first pass.

Pass 1:
Find proportionally frequent itemsets on a random sample
in the same way as the random sampling algorithm
• Use a more conservative threshold (algorithm might fail)

E.g. if the sample is a fraction 𝑝𝑝of the entire file, use
0.8*ps as the support threshold.

Negative border: An itemset that is not frequent in the
sample, but all its immediate subsets are frequent.
•
This is ⋃𝑘𝑘≥1(𝐶𝐶𝑘𝑘∖𝐿𝐿𝑘𝑘) in Apriori
To prepare for pass 2, we record the itemsets which are
either


Frequent in the sample above or

A negative border

{𝐴𝐴, 𝐵𝐵, 𝐶𝐶, 𝐷𝐷} is in the negative border if and only if:
1. It is not frequent in the sample, but
2. All of {𝐴𝐴, 𝐵𝐵, 𝐶𝐶}, {𝐵𝐵, 𝐶𝐶, 𝐷𝐷}, {𝐴𝐴, 𝐶𝐶, 𝐷𝐷}, and {𝐴𝐴, 𝐵𝐵, 𝐷𝐷} are.

Pass 2:
Count all the candidate frequent itemsets from pass 1, as
well as the negative border itemsets.
Two possible outcomes:
1. No itemset in the negative border is frequent in the
whole dataset.
•
Thus, we captured all possible frequent itemsets and
just need to verify the candidates from pass 1.
2. Some itemset in the negative border is frequent in the
whole.
•
Could have missed some larger frequent itemsets,
have to repeat algorithm with a new random sample.
Choose support threshold small enough

Outcome 2: Itemset in the negative
border being frequent

• If there is an itemset S  that is frequent in full data, but not
frequent in the sample (false negative), then the negative
border contains at least one itemset that is frequent in the
whole (algorithm does not terminate)
Proof by contradiction:
• Suppose not.  i.e.
1. There is an itemset S  frequent in the full data but not
frequent in the sample, and
2. Nothing in the negative border is frequent in the full data
• Let T  be a smallest subset of S that is not frequent in the
sample (every subset of T is frequent in the sample)


T  is frequent in the whole (subset of frequent set S).

T  is in the negative border (contradiction)

Pros
1. No false negatives, no false positives.
2. Runtime similar to random sampling, as we only need to
read a sample of the data from disk to memory in pass 1.

Cons
• It might fail if we are not conservative enough with our
threshold for the sample, forcing us to repeat the
algorithm with a new random sample
